common_name: Grenadin Mixed Carnation (Heirloom Fully-Double French Border Carnation Strain)

planting.note: Start indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, since Grenadin is a slow-to-bloom, large-flowered heirloom strain; harden off and transplant after frost danger passes into well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil.

directions: Grenadin is a classic French heirloom border carnation strain dating to the 19th century, grown for its extra-large, fully double, ruffled, spicy clove-scented blooms held on sturdy stems above blue-green grassy foliage, making it a favorite for cutting gardens. The mix produces flowers in shades of scarlet, rose-pink, white, yellow, and bicolors. Sow indoors well before the last frost, as Grenadin is slower to flower than modern bedding carnations, then transplant into full sun and well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-alkaline soil. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, stake or support taller stems, and deadhead to extend bloom; in zones 6-9 plants often persist and rebloom as short-lived perennials.

common_name: Nigrescens Sweet William (Heirloom Dark Chocolate-Maroon Foliage with Crimson-Black Flowers)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in fall for spring bloom in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Nigrescens is an old British heirloom Sweet William and a forerunner of the darker-leaved 'Sooty' selection.

directions: Nigrescens is a long-grown heirloom Sweet William selected for its unusually dark, chocolate-maroon foliage and stems, topped in late spring and early summer by dense, rounded clusters of small, near-black crimson flowers with a light clove fragrance. Grow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil; like other Sweet Williams it behaves as a short-lived biennial or perennial, typically sown one season to bloom the next, and it self-sows readily where content. Deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and to curb volunteer seedlings, which can revert toward greener foliage over generations. The dark foliage makes an effective contrast planted near silver-leaved or chartreuse companions.
